title: Interest and Time
blurb: Compounding, APR vs APY, basis points and what future money is worth today

lessons.title: Compound Interest and the Rule of 72

terms.def: Interest earned on your interest as well as on the money you put in, so growth speeds up over time.
terms.example: $1,000 at 10% a year becomes $1,100 after year 1, then $1,210 after year 2. The extra $10 is interest on interest.

terms.def: Interest paid only on the original amount, never on interest already earned.
terms.example: $1,000 at 5% simple interest earns $50 a year, $150 over 3 years.

terms.def: A shortcut: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years money takes to double.
terms.example: At 8% a year, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.

terms.def: How often interest is added to the balance. More frequent compounding earns slightly more at the same rate.
terms.example: 12% compounded monthly adds 1% each month and ends the year up about 12.68%, not 12%.

cards.title: Interest on interest
cards.body: With simple interest you earn the same amount every year. With compound interest each year's interest joins the balance, so next year you earn interest on a bigger number. The gap is small at first and huge after a few decades.

cards.title: Watch it snowball
cards.body: Put $1,000 in at 10% a year. Year 1: $1,000 × 1.10 = $1,100. Year 2: $1,100 × 1.10 = $1,210. Year 3: $1,331. After 30 years it is about $17,449. Simple interest would give only $1,000 + 30 × $100 = $4,000.

cards.title: The formulas
cards.body: Compound amount: A = P × (1 + r/n)^(n × t), where P is the starting amount, r the yearly rate as a decimal, n how many times a year interest is added and t the number of years. Quick estimate: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate in %. At 6% that is 12 years, at 9% it is 8.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Adding the rate up year by year (10% for 3 years = 30%) is simple-interest thinking. Compounded, 10% for 3 years is 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 − 1 = 33.1%. The longer the time, the bigger this error gets.

checks.prompt: Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 6% a year?
$2,000 earns 5% a year, compounded yearly. What is it worth after 2 years?
checks.explanation: $2,000 × 1.05 = $2,100, then $2,100 × 1.05 = $2,205. The extra $5 is interest earned on the first year's interest.

checks.prompt: Which earns more in a year: 12% compounded yearly or 12% compounded monthly?
checks.explanation: Monthly adds 1% twelve times, so interest starts earning interest sooner. It ends the year up about 12.68%.

terms.def: The yearly interest rate on a loan or account before compounding. On loans it often includes some fees.
terms.example: A card with a 24% APR charges about 2% interest each month.

terms.def: What you really earn or pay in a year once compounding is included.
terms.example: 5% APR compounded monthly is an APY of about 5.12%.

terms.def: One hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). Traders use it so rate changes are never ambiguous.
terms.example: A rate going from 4.25% to 4.50% rose 25 basis points.

terms.def: The plain difference between two percentages, which is not the same as a percent change.
terms.example: A rate rising from 2% to 3% is up 1 percentage point, but up 50% in percent terms.

terms.def: How much something grew or shrank compared with where it started.
terms.example: A stock going from $40 to $46 rose 6 ÷ 40 = 15%.

cards.title: Two numbers for one rate
cards.body: Banks quote the APR, a simple yearly rate. Because interest can be added monthly or daily, what you actually earn or owe in a year is a bit higher: that is the APY. Savings accounts like to advertise the APY because it looks bigger; loans often show the APR because it looks smaller.

cards.title: Turning APR into APY
cards.body: A savings account pays 6% APR, compounded monthly. Each month you earn 6% ÷ 12 = 0.5%. Over a year: 1.005^12 − 1 = 6.17% APY. A loan at 18% APR compounded monthly really costs about 19.56% a year.

cards.title: Speaking trader
cards.body: One basis point (bp) is 0.01%, so 25 bp = 0.25% and 100 bp = 1%. Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old. A rate moving from 2% to 3% is +1 percentage point, or +100 bp, but a 50% increase in percent terms.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Mixing up percentage points and percent. If a rate goes from 4% to 5%, it rose 1 percentage point, which is a 25% rise in relative terms. Another trap: a 50% drop needs a 100% gain to get back to even.

checks.prompt: A central bank raises rates from 4.50% to 4.75%. How many basis points is that?
A stock falls 50%. How much does it then need to rise to get back to where it started?
checks.explanation: $100 falls to $50. Getting from $50 back to $100 means doubling, a 100% gain.

checks.prompt: For the same account, which is higher: the APR or the APY?
checks.explanation: The APY includes compounding, so it is equal to or higher than the APR.

lessons.title: Present Value: Money Now vs Later

terms.def: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can be invested and earn a return.
terms.example: $100 today invested at 5% becomes about $128 in five years, so $100 in five years is worth less than $100 now.

terms.def: What a future amount is worth in today's money, after allowing for the return you could have earned in the meantime.
terms.example: $1,100 a year from now, at a 10% rate, is worth $1,000 today.

terms.def: What money today, or a stream of regular savings, grows to by a future date.
terms.example: $500 a month for 30 years at 7% grows to about $610,000.
terms.formula: FV = P × (1 + r)^t, or for monthly saving C: FV = C × ((1 + i)^N − 1) ÷ i

terms.def: The yearly return used to shrink future money back to today's value. Riskier cash flows get a higher discount rate.
terms.example: A safe government payment might be discounted at 4%, a risky startup's profits at 30%.

cards.title: Why later money is worth less
cards.body: If you can earn 5% a year, then $100 today becomes $105 in a year. So $105 a year from now is only worth $100 today. Turning future money into today's money is called discounting, and the rate you use is the discount rate.

cards.title: Discounting step by step
cards.body: A friend promises you $1,210 in two years. You could earn 10% a year elsewhere. Present value = $1,210 ÷ 1.10 ÷ 1.10 = $1,000. If they offer you $950 today instead, wait for the $1,210, because it is worth $1,000 to you.

cards.title: The formulas
cards.body: Future value: FV = PV × (1 + r)^t. Present value: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^t. A bigger discount rate or a longer wait makes the present value smaller.

cards.title: Common mistake
cards.body: Comparing money at different times as if it were the same. A $30,000 prize paid as $1,000 a year for 30 years is worth far less than $30,000 handed over today.

checks.prompt: You will receive $1,000 in one year. If the discount rate is 10%, what is it worth today?
What happens to the present value of a future payment if the discount rate goes up?
checks.explanation: You divide by a bigger number, so its value today shrinks.

checks.prompt: At a 5% rate, which is worth more today: $1,000 now or $1,050 in two years?
